title: A 14-Year-Old From California Just Won the Scripps Spelling Bee. He Spelled 32 Words in 90 Seconds.
excerpt: Shrey Parikh shattered the spell-off record, defeated Ishaan Gupta in a lightning round, and extended Indian-American dominance of the most famous vocabulary contest.
body:
Shrey Parikh stood at the microphone at DAR Constitution Hall in Washington, D.C., and did what he does every day. He spelled fast. In a 90-second spell-off that will be talked about for years, the 14-year-old from Rancho Cucamonga, California, rattled off 32 correct words out of 35 attempted, clinching the 2026 Scripps National Spelling Bee title with the word "bromocriptine" — a polypeptide alkaloid derived from ergot that mimics the activity of dopamine.

His performance shattered the previous spell-off record set in 2024 by Bruhat Soma, who had correctly spelled 29 of 30 words. When asked how he prepared to spell at that pace, Shrey was characteristically understated: "Spelling fast is what I do every day, so the spell-off kind of came naturally."

The road to the trophy was anything but routine. Shrey first competed at the national level in 2022, finishing tied for 89th place. In 2024, he tied for third. After that near-miss, he took a six-month hiatus from competitive spelling entirely — a deliberate reset that, by his account, allowed him to return with renewed focus and a deeper command of the language patterns that separate good spellers from great ones.

This year's competition drew 247 contestants from all 50 U.S. states, Guam, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Defence Department schools in Europe, and countries including Canada, the Bahamas, Ghana, Nigeria and the United Arab Emirates. After days of elimination rounds, nine finalists remained. Five of them were of Indian origin — a continuation of a trend that has defined the Bee for more than two decades. Since 1999, Indian-American spellers have won 28 of the last 27 competitions that were held, a streak so dominant that it has become inseparable from the event's identity.

The runner-up, 12-year-old Ishaan Gupta of Jersey City, New Jersey, spelled 25 words in his own 90-second round and earned $25,000 in prize money. Third place went to Sarv Dharavane, a 12-year-old from Tucker, Georgia, who earned $15,000 in his second consecutive third-place finish. Kushi Gottimukkala finished fourth.

Shrey's preparation was intensive and systematic. He worked with three coaches, obtained word lists and study guides from multiple sources, and competed year-round in online bees that operate outside the Scripps system. He describes his approach as learning "every language pattern" rather than memorizing individual words — a strategy that pays dividends in the spell-off format, where speed depends on pattern recognition as much as rote recall.

Outside the competition circuit, Shrey is an eighth grader at Day Creek Intermediate School who plays percussion in his school band — snare drum, bass drum, timpani, glockenspiel, marimba. He enjoys tennis, chess, and math, and qualified for the California state Mathcounts Competition. He travels to India regularly to visit his grandparents, a connection that grounds his identity in a way the trophy alone cannot.

The $50,000 top prize came with a commemorative medal, the Scripps Cup, $2,500 from Merriam-Webster, $1,000 in flight credits from Delta Air Lines, and $400 in reference works from Encyclopaedia Britannica.

For the Indian-American community, the Bee has long been more than a vocabulary contest. It is a visible, nationally televised stage where the children of immigrants demonstrate a particular kind of American excellence — disciplined, methodical, earned through years of work that begins long before the cameras arrive. The dominance is not accidental. It is the product of a community infrastructure of coaches, study circles, regional competitions, and a culture that treats academic achievement as a family project.

Shrey's six-month break and return may be the most instructive part of his story. He did not grind harder. He stepped back, recalibrated, and came back sharper. It is a lesson that extends well beyond spelling: sometimes the most productive thing a competitor can do is stop competing for a while.

*Sources: Scripps National Spelling Bee, The Brighter World, Indian Eagle*
